certainty_reasoning: Unlike the rest of this tier, the sentence states a relationship rather than a notice: 'I am practically engaged to a fisherman of extraordinary beauty, age eighteen.' Wilde is asserting a bond, not recording that he saw someone beautiful, so romantic-nonsexual is proposed - the README gloss being that 'nonsexual' describes the evidence and not a finding of fact. No first-person statement of sexual relations appears, so documented-sexual is unavailable. Two things must be weighed against the class and are recorded here rather than buried: first, the register is comic. The sentence answers Wilde's own riff about Ross wanting him to marry 'some sensible, practical, plain, middle-aged boy', and it closes 'So you see there are difficulties' - the joke is on Wilde and on the idea of his remarrying. Second, 'practically engaged' is hedged in its own words, and everything in the sentence is Wilde's assertion: the fisherman's side of it is not recorded, so a mutual connection is documented only in the sense that Wilde claims one. A later check may reasonably prefer desire-expressed on those grounds; this project proposes romantic-nonsexual because the letter's plain sense is a connection already in being, and downgrading it on register alone would let a joke frame delete the content of the claim. AGE: the letter states eighteen, recorded exactly as stated per the module's sensitive-content register; no inference is drawn. Standing caveat for this tier: the record is one-sided by nature. These men left no papers; everything known is what Wilde wrote to a friend. An unrecorded outcome is not evidence of no outcome.
date_label: Stated in a letter of 2 January 1899 from La Napoule, during Wilde's Riviera winter of 1898-99. The letter does not say when the connection began, and no later letter read returns to it.
summary: Writing to Robert Ross from La Napoule on 2 January 1899, Wilde deflected the idea of a second marriage by announcing that he was 'practically engaged' to a local fisherman, whom he called of extraordinary beauty and whose age he gave as eighteen. The man is unnamed and appears nowhere else in the correspondence read; the sentence is at once the only evidence for the connection and a joke at the expense of Wilde's own marriageability.

sources.quote: As regards my marrying again, I am quite sure that you will want me to marry this time some sensible, practical, plain, middle-aged boy, and I don't like the idea at all. Besides I am practically engaged to a fisherman of extraordinary beauty, age eighteen. So you see there are difficulties.
sources.context: Wilde to Robert Ross, 2 January 1899, Napoule - the closing run of a long letter whose earlier paragraphs cover Harold Mellor's daily bicycle visits and the Nice theatre trip.
sources.supports: The whole of the record: Wilde's statement that he is practically engaged to an unnamed Napoule fisherman, with the age the letter gives, in its own comic frame
